title: Miriam's tambourine (Exodus 15:19–21)
hook: Miriam takes a tambourine and the women dance and sing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sea: chariots behind, water ahead, and Moses saying stand still and see. Your line was stand still and see.

Here's a small question hiding in the text. When the Israelites left Egypt in the middle of the night, with dough on their shoulders and no time to pack, who brought the tambourines? Someone, packing in the dark, made room for a drum. On the far shore, with the sea closed behind them, Moses leads the people in a long song of victory. Then the text turns to someone else: a woman who may have stood in the reeds years ago, watching a basket. Now she's holding a hand drum.

In the King James Bible: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame drum, the tof in Hebrew. And notice her title: the text calls her a prophetess. She doesn't just play. She leads, and she calls the song: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." It's almost exactly the first line of Moses's song, turned around. Moses sang, I will sing. Miriam calls, sing ye: two lines, short enough for a whole crowd to shout back. Exodus doesn't name the sister by the river, but tradition says it was Miriam. If so, the girl who watched her baby brother float in the reeds now leads the dancing on the other side of the water. There's a hard side to the song, and Jewish teachers saw it. The Talmud tells of angels in heaven wanting to sing as the Egyptians drowned, and God stopping them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Some readers hear in that story a line between thanks for rescue and joy at someone's death. Christians sing Exodus fifteen too; some churches use it as a canticle in morning prayer. Music, it turns out, was one of the things worth carrying out of Egypt.
screen: `MIRIAM THE PROPHETESS.` · `TIMBRELS AND DANCES.` · `THE GIRL BY THE RIVER, YEARS LATER.` · `THANKS, NOT JOY AT DEATH.` · then, large: `SING YE TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been brought through, an illness, a bad year, a long wait that ended, and give it a beat: tap your knee, the table or your chest, slow at first, then let it grow the way Miriam's drum drew the women after her. Stand and sway if you like. If you pray, let the rhythm be your thanks to God; if you don't, let it be thanks anyway.
Miriam's tambourine. The hand drum Miriam the prophetess played on the far shore of the sea, leading the women in dance and song.
Your line: sing to the lord. A song can be carried a long way. That's day three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some churches sing the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) as a canticle at morning prayer or at the Easter Vigil, and in some Christian communities drums and dancing are part of worship.

original.note: Hebrew: a hand drum or frame drum, the timbrel Miriam played.

trapdoor: what you thought: Miriam played a tambourine at a victory party.
what it means: a prophetess leads the women in thanks for rescue, and a later Jewish story has God stop the angels from singing as the Egyptians drown.
what a scholar hears: Miriam's couplet repeats Moses's opening line in 15:1 almost word for word, but turns 'I will sing' into 'sing ye', a call to everyone.

chat.says: Who led the singing after Israel crossed the sea?
options: Moses sang first, then Miriam the prophetess took a drum and led the women in dance.
Aaron led it, since he was the speaker Moses relied on back in Egypt.
The priests led it, since only priests were allowed to sing to God.
chat.meaning: Moses led a long song; then Miriam, called a prophetess, took a timbrel and led the women: sing ye to the Lord.

timbrel.meaning: a hand drum or frame drum

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess' (superlative not in the text), 'now she's old' (no age given), and the 'many scholars / oldest poetry' claim from the teach and trapdoor, replaced with the text's own 'I will sing' / 'sing ye' turn; the Talmud's angels are now framed as a story some readers draw on, not a narrator ruling that Israel's song was never joy at death; 'for centuries' and 'many churches' softened; hook no longer echoes day 387's 'grab what's in your hands' line.
The Talmud passage (Megillah 10b / Sanhedrin 39b) is paraphrased; confirm wording and citation.
Miriam as 'the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess' (15:20). Confirm.
'Now she's old': by Exodus chronology Moses is about eighty (Exodus 7:7) and Miriam older; the text does not give her age. Confirm the phrasing.
Scholarly views on the antiquity of Exodus 15 and the priority of Miriam's song are presented as views, not facts.
The Song of the Sea as a canticle (e.g. 'Cantemus Domino' in Lauds, Anglican and Lutheran usage). Confirm.
